ALMONTE; ONT.

Local News.

—Saturday was the shortest day of the year.

—Mr. A. K. McLean of Ottawa was a visitor in town last week.

—Miss Lizzie Bowes paid a visit to Carleton Place friends last week.

—Mr. Ed. Rea of Landis, Sask., is visiting at his home in Ramsay.

We wish all a Merry Christmas and Happy New Year—From O’Reilly’s.

—Mr. Archie Kean has returned home from the university of Ottawa.

—Mr. Milton Cochrane, of the O. A.C., Guelph, is home for the holidays.

—Mr. C. E. Boyce of Cobalt is spending a couple of weeks at his home here.

—Mr. and Mrs. W. M. Young of Detroit are guests of friends in town and vicinity.

—Miss Grace McGregor is spending the Christmas vacation at her home in Balderson.

—Mrs. Geo. Bowes and Master Lester are spending this week with Carleton Place friends.

—Mr. and Mrs. W. N. Acton are spending the Christmas holidays with Oxford mills friends.

—Mr. T. J. O’Donnell of the High school staff, is spending his vacation at his home at Kingscote.

—Dr. P. Drummond of Grant, Mich., spent Christmas with his mother, Mrs. P. Drummond, sr.

—Miss K. McDonald of Pembroke is spending her vacation with her parents, Mr. and Mrs. L. McDonald.

—Miss Winnie Garvin of Munster will spend the Christmas vacation with her mother, Mrs. D. Garvin.

—Miss Edna McCaughan of Ottawa is spending a few days with her parents, Mr. and Mrs. W. McCaughan.

—Messrs. P. Earnshaw, E. Robb, F. Fraser and E. Paul of Queen’s are home for the Christmas vacation.

Mr. T. S. Leger will resume his dancing class on Tuesday evening, the 31st, in the F.M.T.A. hall at 8 p.m.

Don’t forget Dr. Bell’s lecture on Thursday evening of this week. It will be well worth your while to hear it.

—Miss Violet Young, nurse-in-training at Stamford, Conn., hospital, is
—Miss Violet Young, nurse-in-training at Stamford, Conn., hospital, is spending the Christmas holidays at her home here.

—Mrs. W. H. Lanning and Miss Lorna Lanning and Misses Alice and Agnes Gilmour of Montreal are guests of Mrs. R. Gilmour.

—Mr. Chas. Clark of Detroit and his son, Mr. H. Clark of Lorraine, Ohio, were called home last week, owing to the illness of Mrs. C. Clark.

—Mr. M. L. McLellan, of the P.S. staff, left last week for his home at Streetsville. Before leaving his pupils presented him with a leather collar box.

—Miss Mary Kean won the prize of the senior class in St. Mary’s Sunday school, it being a gold cross, presented by her teacher, Miss Theresa O’Heare.

—Have you made anybody happy this happy Christmas time? If not, it is not altogether too late yet. You know somebody who is not so well off as you are—give him a boost.

—Miss Margaret Dunfield, of the R.M. hospital staff, has gone home to nurse her father, Mr. Thos. Dunfield, of Renfrew, who has had to undergo an operation for an abscess.

—While Mr. Arthur Steele and sisters of Bennie’s Corners were returning home from church at Blakeney last Sunday morning their horse got frightened and started to run, but fortunately the driver hung on to the lines and managed to control it after a race of a half mile or more, with no more serious result than a broken cutter.

—The Christmas tree and entertainment in connection with St. Paul’s Sunday school will be held in the town hall on Thursday, Jan. 2nd. A lecture entitled, “A Holiday in England,” illustrated with lantern views, will be given by the Rev. A. W. MacKay, rector of All Saints’ church, Ottawa. There will also be a short musical program.

—The new sheds for St. Paul’s church are now under construction. They are being erected on the corner of Martin and Brougham streets, the entrance being on the latter street. The sheds are commodious and when completed will be comfortable. They will be very much appreciated by the people who come in
and when completed will be comfortable. They will be very much appreciated by the people who come in from the country to service.

Doing Something Different.

This year instead of giving your boy and girl the usual list of Christmas gifts, suppose you hand them a check sufficient to pay a course at the Brockville Business College. You’ll not have to wait long for an appreciation of your good judgment. New term opens Jan. 6th, 1913.

Doll Contest.

Taber & Co.’s Doll Contest was closed Christmas Eve and the following little girls are now the proud possessors of the beautiful dolls which have been displayed in their windows for the past few weeks: Marjorie Scott, Marjorie MacFarlane, Emily Fallas, Annie Camelon and Ruth Barclay.

A Narrow Escape.

A young man from the Shawville neighborhood, who had been in the west and was on his way home, stepped off the car to the platform on Sunday evening when the Winnipeg train, upon which he was a passenger, stopped at the station. As the train started he ran forward to get
on again, but was met by a closed vestibule car. He tried to run ahead to another car, but slipped and fell between the station platform and the train, and the wonder is that he was not killed. He had presence of mind enough to lie still, and escaped with a badly injured foot and ankle. A doctor was called and fixed the injured member as comfortably as possible, and the young man proceeded homeward on the Soo train. The ankle was so badly swollen that it was difficult to decide just what the extent of the injury was without a close examination, possible only after the swelling had subsided.

Temperance Meetings.

A meeting will be held in the town hall on Friday evening, Jan. 3rd, at which it is expected that addresses will be given by speakers from Toronto and elsewhere. Then on Sunday, Jan. 5th, the pulpits in the various Protestant churches will be occupied by special speakers from outside the town. In addition a mass meeting will be held in the town hall at 3.30 o'clock on Sunday, at which good speakers will be present, and to which everybody is invited.

A Generous Sub.

Two little boys in town, with a strong and abiding faith in good old Saint Nicholas, by laborious effort
each penned a note to Santa Claus telling him what they would like him to bring to them for their Christmas presents. These were addressed to him and mailed at the postoffice, with a broadly smiling Santa Claus stamp in lieu of that recognized by His Majesty as an equivalent for his services in the transportation of such missives. But all the same it reached a destination which was just as good as Santa Claus' land, and Mr. Thoburn had the pleasure of playing Mr. Bountiful for old St. Nick, which he did in a generous manner, and there were at least two happy and satisfied little boys when Christmas morning broke.

Hartrick—McDowall.

A very pretty wedding took place on Thursday evening, Dec. 19th, at the home of Mr. and Mrs. W. J. McDowall, when their daughter, Minnie J., was united in bonds of holy matrimony to Mr. Albert Hartrick of Hartney, Man., Rev. E. P. H. King, of the Baptist church, officiating. At five o'clock, to the strains of music from the orchestra, in which Mr. W. R. McDowall, brother of the bride, and daughters, Eunice and Ruth, took the leading part, the bridal party entered the drawing room and took their places under an arch of evergreens, roses and carnations. The bride wore a beautiful white satin gown with pearl trimmings and carried a bouquet of white roses and lilies of the valley. Little Miss Viola McDowall, niece of the bride, made a charming flower girl, dressed in white and carrying a basket of pink carnations. After the ceremony the guests repaired to the dining room, which was prettily decorated with roses and carnations, where a sumptuous wedding supper was served. The toast to the bride was proposed by Rev. Mr. King and replied to in a very pleasing manner by the groom. Many were the good wishes expressed by the guests. After a social hour Mr. and Mrs. Hartrick left for Carleton Place, where they took train en route for Ottawa and other points of interest. Later they will proceed to Vancouver, B.C., where they intend to reside. Going away the bride wore

The person who dares to follow his or her own independent judgment, but runs perpetually to others for advice, becomes an intellectual dwarf. Such a ‘one is borne about the world as a mere insignificant cipher.

It is said that a lobster when left high and dry among the rocks, has not instinct and energy enough to work his way back to the sea, but waits for the sea to come to him. If it does not come he remains where he is and dies. The world is full of human lobsters. People stranded on the rocks, who instead of putting forth their own energies, are waiting for some billow of good fortune to set them afloat.

One of the most disgusting sights in the world is a young man or woman with broad shoulders and a hundred and fifty pounds of bone and muscle, standing at ease, and longing for help. Pecuniary help to a beginner, is the devil’s blessing—to be deprecated, not coveted.

God never intended that strong, independent beings should be reared by clinging to others, like the ivy to the oak for support. The difficulties, hardships, and trials of life—the obstacles one encounters on the road to fortune are positive blessings. They knit our muscles more firmly, and teach us self reliance, just as, by wrestling with an athlete who is superior to us, we increase our own strength, and learn the secret of his skill. All difficulties come to us like the lion which met Samson: The first time we encounter them they roar and gnash their teeth, but once subdued we find a nest of honey in them.

A Handsome Gift.

Death of Mrs. James McLean.

A telephone message on Saturday night to James G. McLean of Lanark conveyed the sad news of the serious illness of his mother, Mrs. James McLean, McDonald’s Corners, and on Sunday night she passed peacefully away to her long rest. Deceased had reached the age of eighty-two, and her death was due to declining years and a general break up of the system. Mrs. McLean, whose maiden name was Kate Gunn, daughter of the late John Gunn, was born in Lanark township, near Hopetown. About sixty years ago she married James McLean, and their union was

C. Campbell, San Diego, Cal., and Mrs. Andrew Paul, Dalhousie, who survive. Mr. McLean died two years ago last April.

Development of Almonte Power.

A meeting of considerable importance to the town was held in the Council Chamber on Saturday afternoon, when the waterpower owners, represented by Messrs. James and Alex. Rosamond, Jas. W. Wylie, H. Taylor, E. N. Spohr of Penman’s Limited, W. Glover of the Mississippi Iron Works, W. Thoburn, M.P., and the Electric Light Commissioners, by Dr. Metcalf, Dr. Young, and Messrs. Geo. Bradford and L. W. Shipman. The meeting, which was presided over by Mayor Pittard, was the result of the visit of Mr. J. D. McRae, C.E., of Ottawa, who was here last week, and was called to discuss the feasibility of unifying the water powers, or of arriving at some understanding whereby the development of more power might be secured. The matter was widely discussed from a variety of viewpoints, with a desire to obtain all the information possible regarding the work. The experience of Renfrew was cited, where the town had acquired all the waterpowers, and had combined these and now supply power to manufacturers and others as they require it, at a rate of $22 per horse-power per year. Conditions in Renfrew are different from those existing in Almonte, but it was felt by those present that it was a desirable thing that something should be done to make the development of power for manufacturing purposes a possibility. Without definite information, however, very little could be done, and Mr. McRae, who was present, was authorized to proceed with a survey of the whole ground, and submit a report thereon at a meeting to be held later on. The question is one of vital importance to Almonte, and it
is to be hoped that some scheme may be arrived at that will result in bringing about the desired improvements.

Stanley–Rath.

A very pretty wedding was solemnized at 2.30 on the 24th inst., in St. George’s church, Clayton, by Rev. Mr. Turley, when Mr. Clifford Stanley, a prosperous young farmer of Cedar Hill, and Miss Annie Rath, youngest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Alex. Rath, were united in the holy bonds of matrimony. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a gown of cream duchesse satin, with a long net veil prettily arranged over her hair, and carrying a prayer book richly bound in white. Miss Maggie McMunn acted as bridesmaid, and wore a dress of shot silk, blue and green, with large black hat, and carrying a bouquet of pink carnations and maiden hair fern. Mr. Herbert Stanley, cousin of the groom, performed the duties of groomsman. The presents received show the popularity in which the young couple are held, among them being substantial cheques from friends of both the bride and groom. The groom’s gift to the bride was a handsome fur-lined coat and to the bridesmaid a gold brooch. After the ceremony the bridal party, accompanied by the near relatives, drove to the home of the bride’s parents, where a sumptuous wedding dinner awaited them. After full justice had been done at the tables, the bridal party, with a few of the young people, drove to the home of the groom, where a reception was held and a few hours of social pleasure were spent. The bride’s travelling dress was of navy paillette silk with large black hat. The many friends of Mr. and Mrs. Stanley wish them a happy and prosperous journey through life.

FRIDAY, DEC. 27th, 1912.

Pakenham

Gathered by Gazette

Mrs. S. Allison visited Ottawa over Sunday last.

Rev. W. T. McKenzie paid Ottawa a visit on Monday of this week.

Mr. Lorne Lesage arrived home on Monday of this week for the holidays.

Mr. James Phee injured his leg a few weeks ago and it is still causing him trouble.

Mrs. P. McV. Russell, who has been ill for the past week or more, is progressing favorably.

Miss Jean Connery of Cedar Hill, who has been attending Ottawa Normal school, is home for the Christmas holidays.

Mr. Arthur Steele, of Guelph Agricultural College is spending the Christmas holidays at the parental home at Bennie's Corners.

On Saturday of last week Mr. P. Noonan shipped some 50 odd three-year old fatted steers of his own feeding to Montreal, for Christmas and New Year's beef.

See the new assortment skates at A. H. Tait's. See the assortment axes A. H. Tait is showing. Come and get the big bargains offered by A. H. Tait in all lines tin and hardware for balance this month.

Much sympathy is felt for the Graham family in Pakenham, as Mrs. Graham has been quite ill the past couple of weeks and last week Miss Graham was laid aside by a severe attack of pleurisy, taking away much of the pleasure of the Christmas time.

Among the homecomers the past week are Miss Bessie Scott from Toronto Conservatory of Music; Mr. John Henderson from the Northwest, home for the winter to visit among his many friends in this district; Mr. J. Dean also from the Northwest for the winter.

Mr. J. A. Francis left on Friday of last week for Ottawa, where he was married to Miss Mary McCreary of Arnprior, and the young couple are having a honeymoon trip to New York and other American and Canadian cities. They are expected to return next week.

St. Andrew's church Sunday school, instead of holding the usual Christmas tree entertainment indulged in a
St. Andrew's church Sunday school, instead of holding the usual Christmas tree entertainment indulged in a sleigh ride on Friday evening of last week, followed by tea in the dining room of the church, after which a short program of recitations, etc., was held in the Sunday school room, and a most pleasant evening spent by the teachers and scholars.

Santa Claus has been good to the pastor of St. Andrew's congregation this week. On Monday last Rev. W. T. McKenzie, on his return from Ottawa, found that good farmer friends on the west side of Pakenham, belonging to St. Andrew's church, had clubbed together and sent the Rev. gentleman a good load of oats for his horse. Mr. McKenzie thanks his friends for their thoughtful consideration.

On Sunday evening last Rev. W. Howitt, the pastor, had a change in the usual service, having Rev. W. T. McKenzie of St. Andrew's Presbyterian church assist, each of the pastors giving short addresses. The choir gave some special music. Mrs. J. J. Groves sang a solo and the orchestra of the church rendered two or three pieces in their usual masterly style, with Miss Bessie Scott as organist.

A. H. Tait wishes to heartily and gratefully thank his many customers for their liberal patronage the past year, which has been one of the very best in his forty-three years' business history in Pakenham and would most respectfully announce that by continuous, kindly, courteous fair dealing wishes to merit and receive a yet greater patronage for 1913. Wishing you one and all a very Happy, Pleasant and Prosperous New Year.

On Friday evening of last week Dr. W. H. Gemmill of Pakenham gave a temperance address at Fitzroy Harbor, in aid of Local Option in Fitzroy township. He was accompanied to the Harbor by Messrs. A. S. Wilkinson, James Howe and A. H. Tait. The Dr. gave a most interesting and instructive address, convincing some of the wavering ones in the audience that Local Option was for their benefit and for the benefit of all, even the liquor seller himself. The contest goes on daily and the temperance men have been much cheered by their canvass for local option.

Pakenham Township Council.

The council met at Pakenham on December 14th, at one o'clock p.m. Members all present. The minutes of the last meeting were read and sustained.

Communication from James Headrick, respecting a road on the 3rd line at lot 22, was read.

Report of John McGill, on one sheep and one lamb killed by dogs, was read.

Accounts were read from John Givens, $18.05; F. H. Somerton, work on roads, $23.75; Almonte Gazette, printing, $5.14; Almonte Times, printing voters' lists, etc., $55.41; J. S. Moir, blasters friend, $6.64; M. Millar and the clerk, repairs on 8th line bridge, $51.50.

Mr. Millar gave notice that he would at the present session of council introduce a bylaw to appoint the places for holding the municipal election, and deputy returning officers and poll clerks therefor.

A SHEET should always be provided for children’s Christmas games. Arranged as a screen it serves many purposes besides shadow pictures and lantern shows.

Two capital games are played in this manner. For one an opening about six inches wide should be cut in the sheet at a convenient height for different persons to stand and show only their eyes. No light should be back of the sheet, and the company seated in front must guess whose eyes are staring at them.

A variation of this idea may be even more amusing because it affords opportunity for misleading the guessers. Instead of an opening the sheet is drawn up a few inches from the floor in order to show the feet of those who stand behind it. Boys accordingly put on skirts, and girls slip their hands into their fathers’ shoes, getting down on all fours in order to deceive.

Another mirth provoking trick for children of all ages and one that will be heartily appreciated by adults is called mesmerism. Blacken the center of the under side of a small plate by holding it over the flame of a candle, being careful not to soil the edge or top. Put this plate upon another and place them in front of you. The person to be mesmerized must be seated so that by no possibility can he see his reflection in the glass, but must be in full view of the audience.

The mesmerist says impressively: “You must look me steadily in the eye all the time. Don’t remove your eyes an instant from my face, but do just as I do slowly—see (picking up the blackened plate and handing it to the victim so that the black is toward the spectators). Hold it so (taking up the other plate and holding it with the concave side toward himself). Now this way (rubbing his finger round and round the back of the clean plate and the one who is mesmerized drawing his round the blackened one unconscious of its condition), now so (drawing the finger down the right cheek). Never mind how they laugh. You must not look down. Steady. Now again” (rubbing the finger as before and drawing it across the other cheek). The operation may be repeated until the face of the one mesmerized pre-
sents a most comical appearance and the audience is convulsed with laughter.

SNIGGLE THE SPRIG.

“Sniggle the sprig” means simply snare or catch the sprig. Any bit of green plant will do for the latter, and any number of children can play the game. Some one who is not playing hides the sprig, and all search for it. When found it has to be carried to a fancifully trimmed pole and tied there. This is no easy matter, for the sprig must first go through the hands of every player, and it is every one’s aim to catch it before it reaches the pole. No attempt to do this can be made, however, until the sprig has returned to the hands of the finder and that player is running for the goal.

In the midst of the general search, when the finder has found the sprig, he approaches his nearest neighbor and quietly hands it to him. At the same time he gives his neighbor No. 2, which means that this one is the second person to hold it. The latter in turn as carefully passes it on and numbers this player a unit higher. So the game goes on until the last of the players has held the sprig. This one knows that he is the last, for the reason that before the game began a count was taken, and each participant knows just how many persons are taking part.

When the number is given to each player the first name of the finder is whispered also. As soon as the last player receives the sprig he passes it to the finder, who at once runs for the goal with it. All follow and give chase except the last player, who is not permitted to run.

In the scrimmage that follows the sprig may be snatched a dozen times. That one is victor who succeeds in placing it on the pole. Should it be the finder, then his triumph will have been so much the greater, for he will have had the most difficulties to overcome in doing this.
